A detection perimeter behind and above the goal so a script can resolve shots wide, over, or out of play
A large scoreboard structure in the stadium carrying the score, the round, and the sudden-death and must-score states
The seated crowd and the benched squads, and the ground they occupy

mechanics: Solo vs AI with Casual, Competitive and Expert difficulties
Two Player Match alternating striker and goalkeeper
Server owns match state, score, timers, order, trajectory and result
Five kicks each then sudden death, with all eleven players kicking before anyone repeats
Player ratings 1-100 for penalty skill, power, technique, composure, chip skill; keepers also reaction, reach, handling, anticipation
Pressure shrinks the timing windows and is shown with heartbeat, crowd hush and camera tightening
Striker flow: shot type, aim, power minigame, contact minigame, then an uncertainty ellipse
Six goalkeeper save regions with guess-early or wait-and-react strategies
AI must not read private striker input
Mobile-first controls with mouse, keyboard and gamepad support
Main menu, mode and difficulty selection, tutorial, result screen, rematch
Whistle, crowd ambience, hush, kick, net, glove, post, cheers, groans, heartbeat and celebration audio
Balance targets: 70-80% scoring on Competitive, matches lasting 5-8 minutes
Fifteen required tests before reporting what is complete or partial
notes: Full Stadium preset kept for the dressing, but its space-bounded shape was replaced by range-directed: the prompt explicitly builds only the penalty shootout, which is a directed range at a single target rather than a field with a foul perimeter. Route quoted is the shape actually used.
P0 + tiered comes from the bleachers only; the genre note warns stands build flat unless the height is captured.
The prompt is overwhelmingly rules, UI, AI and networking. Triage put all of it in mechanics; the layout job is one penalty end of one stadium and is small on purpose.
Six save regions and the aim target are subdivisions of the goal mouth. They are spatial but not geometry, and no option expresses a grid inside a scoring volume - flagged rather than invented.

constraints.text: Do not use FIFA, World Cup, real teams, real players, sponsor logos, official kits, or protected tournament branding. Use fictional teams, players, badges, uniforms, and stadium graphics.
Build a polished vertical slice focused only on penalty shootouts. Do not add a full soccer match, progression, currency, shops, quests, or monetization.
Prioritize reliability over complicated custom assets.

notes_for_us: A 20 KB prompt whose layout content is four sentences. Triage handles it correctly, but mechanics ends up holding a design document, and nothing caps or structures that array - one entry per gameplay statement would run to fifty entries here.

range-directed is filed under Sports for golf and archery and is the right shape for a penalty shootout, which nothing in the genre file suggests. The Target Sport note lists bowling, golf, archery, darts; adding 'penalty shootout, free throw, field goal' would save the judgement call.
The prompt spends a third of its words on prohibitions (no real branding, no monetization, no full match). constraints held them, which is the first field in this handoff that has ever been able to.

image_prompt.text: Wardrobes, understairs recesses and furniture gaps through the house where you break the monster's line of sight - at least 4 studs on the way in
The heavy locked door the five keys open, set into the outer wall of the house
Little scraps of paper left in your natural sightline - on tables, on shelves, pinned to walls - each one telling you where a key is
Rooms and closets off the main corridors that can be shut behind you

layout_placement.text: The locked door that opens once all five keys are in, acting as the escape trigger
Five keys hidden around the house in concealed spots that need searching for
The keyholes on the door that accept each key as it is found
Where the scary monster enters the house and the corridors and stairs it patrols
The paper clues, placed so each one is findable from a normal walking route

mechanics: A monster chases you
Five keys open one door
Clues tell you where the keys are
notes: Escape preset, which is the keys-and-a-locked-door house exactly. warren-looping kept: the genre makes zero dead ends a hard property because a cornered corridor makes a chase unfair, so P6 stands.

building-interior is kept from the preset but priced out of the route: play never leaves the house, so there is no outside-to-inside transition and its P3 would be wrong. Recorded in preset_rejected rather than dropped.

facade-clue is stretched from a feature wall to loose paper notes. The ID's concept is clue-hosting and nothing else covers a note, but the wording assumes architecture and the prompt's clues are props.
count 5 carried on the keys; the prompt states the number and nothing else in the handoff could hold it.

notes_for_us: The clue-to-key relationship is the actual mechanic - note A tells you key B is in room C - and the handoff can say there are clues and there are keys but not that a given clue points at a given key. Five keys and five clues placed independently is a different game.

Hiding places are the one thing this map has to have and cover-los arrived from the preset rather than from the prompt, because the prompt says 'chases' and never says 'hide'. The step 0 forward-reasoning rule covers it, but the label lands in preset_derived and understates how prompt-driven it is.

'Massive house' is a stated extent with no stated contents, which is the scale rule's own trigger case - and the answer it lands on (Block) is the band that will not draw the furniture the keys are hidden behind.
